title: Trees and Binary Search Trees
summary: Trees and their vocabulary, binary trees, the binary search tree property, recursive insert, search and delete including the two-child case, in-order, pre-order, post-order and level-order traversal, height and balance, why balanced trees like Java's TreeMap guarantee O(log n), and heaps for priority queues.

cards.q: What does an in-order traversal of a BST produce?
cards.a:
The keys in sorted order

In-order visits left, node, right; with smaller keys on the left that is ascending order. Root first is pre-order, level by level is level-order.

cards.q: Why can inserting 1, 2, 3, ..., n into a plain BST be slow?
cards.a:
Each key becomes the right child of the last, so the tree is a chain

The chain has height about n, so operations become O(n): a plain BST does not rebalance, and sorted input turns it into a linked list. Self-balancing trees like `TreeMap` keep the height O(log n).

cards.q: Deleting a node with two children replaces its key with:
cards.a:
the smallest key in its right subtree

The in-order successor keeps the BST property; the largest key in the left subtree would also work.
